name: Sigurd the Crusader
summary: Norwegian king known as Sigurd the Crusader, remembered for his expedition to Jerusalem.
overview: Sigurd of Norway, often called Sigurd the Crusader, was king of Norway and the first Scandinavian king to take part personally in crusading in the eastern Mediterranean. His journey to Jerusalem made him a distinctive figure in Norwegian and crusading history.

Born around 1090, with no reliable birthplace used here, Sigurd ruled in Norway after a long expedition through England, Iberia, Sicily, and Jerusalem. He died in Oslo in 1130, and his death helped open a period of civil conflict in Norway.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sigurd of Norway, often called Sigurd the Crusader, was king of Norway and the first Scandinavian king to take part personally in crusading in the eastern Mediterranean. His journey to Jerusalem made him a distinctive figure in Norwegian and crusading history.

Born around 1090, with no reliable birthplace used here, Sigurd ruled in Norway after a long expedition through England, Iberia, Sicily, and Jerusalem. He died in Oslo in 1130, and his death helped open a period of civil conflict in Norway.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Sigurd was born around 1090, probably into the Norwegian royal dynasty, but his exact birthplace is not securely known. He was a son of Magnus Barefoot and grew up in a political culture shaped by royal travel, war bands, and competing claims to kingship.
Norway in this period was connected to the wider North Sea and Atlantic world, with ties to Denmark, England, and the Norse settlements beyond Scandinavia.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Sigurd the Crusader is remembered in the saga tradition, above all in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, as a king of restless ambition and grand gestures, whose journey to the Holy Land gave him a prestige no earlier Norwegian ruler had claimed. The sagas present him as proud, magnificent, and conscious of his own standing, celebrated for leading a fleet to Jerusalem, fighting in Iberia and the Mediterranean, and being received with honour in Constantinople, where he reportedly left his ships to the Byzantine emperor.

The same tradition, however, also preserves a darker strand: episodes of instability and harsh temper in his later years, including quarrels and moments of erratic behaviour that the sagas record with unusual frankness for a celebrated king. Because these accounts were written more than a century after his death, the specific incidents must be treated as saga memory rather than documented fact.

What the tradition consistently conveys is a ruler defined by the crusading achievement that set him apart, combined with a pride and volatility that his admirers did not entirely conceal. The crusade made his reputation; the saga writers, working from oral memory, gave him a personality to match its grandeur and its strains.

contentSections.title: As king of Norway and crusader
paragraphs: Sigurd became king in 1103, sharing Norway with his brothers Øystein and Olaf after their father Magnus Barefoot was killed in Ireland. In the autumn of 1107 he sailed from Norway on the expedition that gave him his byname: according to the saga, about 60 ships and some 5,000 men, the first time a European king went to the Holy Land in person. The fleet spent its first winter in England at the court of Henry I of England and sailed south in the spring of 1108.

The next winter was spent in Galicia, near Santiago de Compostela, where the saga says the local lord refused to sell the Norwegians food and Sigurd stormed his castle and plundered it. In the spring of 1109 the fleet worked down the coast of Muslim-held Portugal: it captured eight galleys, took a castle at Sintra, won a fight at Lisbon, which the saga calls half Christian and half heathen, sacked a town it calls Alkasse, probably Alcácer do Sal, and beat a Muslim squadron near the Strait of Gibraltar. These episodes are known chiefly from Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla and the older skaldic verse it quotes, so their details should be read as saga memory.

In the Mediterranean the Norwegians raided the Balearic Islands, the first recorded Christian attack on them. On Formentera they fought a large band of defenders sheltering in a cave, the most fully described fight of the whole voyage, and took what the saga calls the greatest treasure of the expedition, before attacking Ibiza and Menorca; they left well-fortified Majorca alone. In Sicily, then a county rather than a kingdom, they were welcomed by the young count Roger II.

In the summer of 1110 the fleet reached Acre, and Baldwin I of Jerusalem received Sigurd and rode with him to Jerusalem and the Jordan. Baldwin then asked for help against the ports still in Muslim hands, and Sigurd joined him at the siege of Sidon, which the Fatimids had refortified. Baldwin's army invested the town by land while the Norwegian fleet blockaded it from the sea, keeping away Fatimid ships from Tyre, and a Venetian fleet arrived to help. Sidon surrendered after about 47 days, late in 1110, on terms that let those who wished to leave go safely, and it became a lordship of the kingdom of Jerusalem. As a reward Sigurd was given a splinter of the True Cross, on condition that he take it to the shrine of Saint Olaf and promote the faith at home.

From the Levant Sigurd sailed to Constantinople in 1111, where Alexios I Komnenos received him with great ceremony. He left the emperor his ships and their gilded figureheads, and many of his men stayed on in Byzantine service, while he went home overland through the Balkans and central Europe. Back in Norway he was the most celebrated king of his age, and his rule at home combined church patronage, building and royal authority, though saga memory remembered the crusade above everything else.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died in Oslo in 1130 after a reign remembered for crusading, building projects, and later instability.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Sigurd is remembered as the Norwegian crusader king, a ruler whose journey placed Norway within the wider crusading world. His story shows that the crusades reached far beyond France, England, and the Mediterranean core.
His reputation depends heavily on saga and later historical writing, so the broad outline is useful while details should be handled cautiously.

timeline.title: Born

timeline.title: Becomes king of Norway
timeline.description: Rules jointly after Magnus Barefoot's death.

timeline.title: Sails on crusade
timeline.description: Leaves Norway with a large fleet, by the saga's count about 60 ships.

timeline.title: Winter in England
timeline.description: The fleet winters at the court of Henry I of England.

timeline.title: Winter in Galicia
timeline.description: Storms a local lord's castle near Santiago de Compostela after a quarrel over food.

timeline.title: Fighting on the Portuguese coast
timeline.description: Takes a castle at Sintra, fights at Lisbon and sacks Alcácer do Sal, as the saga tells it.

timeline.title: Raids the Balearic Islands
timeline.description: Wins the cave fight on Formentera and attacks Ibiza and Menorca.

timeline.title: Lands at Acre
timeline.description: Received by Baldwin I of Jerusalem, with whom he rides to Jerusalem and the Jordan.

timeline.title: Helps take Sidon
timeline.description: His fleet blockades Sidon while Baldwin besieges it by land; the town surrenders after about 47 days.

timeline.title: Enters Constantinople
timeline.description: Arrives at the Byzantine capital with great ceremony.

timeline.title: Campaigns in Smaland
timeline.description: Associated with a campaign sometimes described as a crusade.

predecessor.note: His father; Sigurd ruled jointly with Øystein I until 1123

successor.note: Norway passed to the rival kings Magnus IV and Harald Gille, whose contested succession opened a century of Norwegian civil war.
